title.en: Economics: Gross Domestic Product and its Growth: an Introduction

text.en: Asha asked how we know whether the whole country is growing. "By GDP," said her teacher.

Gross Domestic Product measures final output produced inside an economy over a specified period. Gross National Product, also called Gross National Income in modern accounts, equals GDP plus primary income received from abroad minus primary income paid abroad. Net National Product subtracts depreciation. Per capita measures divide an aggregate by population.
The expenditure, income and production approaches view the same economic activity from different sides. Nominal GDP values output at current prices. Real GDP is adjusted for price changes and is used to measure output growth.
Agriculture and other primary activities, industry and services all contribute to output. State accounts measure production within states, including Tamil Nadu. Additional indicators help assess how widely growth benefits people and what it means for resources and the environment.
Gross Domestic Product, or G D P, measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy during a specified period.

text.en: Economic growth is usually measured by the percentage rise in real G D P. A rise in nominal G D P alone can reflect higher prices.

text.en: Real GDP is adjusted for price changes and nominal GDP is not.

board.text: services sector

text.en: The textbook groups production into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors. Services form the tertiary sector and make a substantial contribution to India’s economy.

board.text: GDP

text.en: Growth can be assessed alongside who benefits and how resources are used. State accounts provide a measure called Gross State Domestic Product for comparisons within a state.

board.text: GNP

text.en: A factory’s output contributes to the domestic economy where its production occurs. The owner’s residence is a separate question for national income.

board.text: GDP measures production inside the boundary

text.en: GDP measures output over time. A quarterly figure describes production in a quarter, while an annual figure describes a full year.

board.text: The period could be a quarter or a year

text.en: A loaf sold to a household is final output. Flour bought by the bakery is an intermediate input to the loaf.

board.text: Final goods and services are counted

text.en: If you count the loaf’s full selling price and then add the flour’s price again, you count some input value twice.

board.text: Avoid counting the same value twice

text.en: A bakery sells a loaf for one hundred rupees. If its intermediate inputs cost sixty rupees, the bakery adds forty rupees of value.

board.text: Value added measures a producer’s contribution

text.en: Production creates output. That activity generates incomes, and final users spend on output. Each approach views the economy from a different side.

board.text: The production, income and expenditure approaches are linked

text.en: In the school model, add consumption, investment, government spending on goods and services, and exports. Subtract imports to focus on domestic production.

board.text: Expenditure groups final spending

text.en: Some goods bought by households or firms were produced abroad. Subtraction avoids treating foreign production already included in spending as domestic output.

board.text: Why imports are subtracted

text.en: Wages and operating income are important examples. National accountants also make adjustments for taxes and subsidies as appropriate to the measure.

board.text: The income approach tracks income generated in production

text.en: To move from GDP to gross national income, add primary income received from abroad and subtract primary income paid to non-residents.

board.text: National income considers residents’ primary income

text.en: Machinery and buildings wear out or lose value as they are used. A net product measure subtracts an estimate of this consumption of fixed capital.

board.text: Gross and net differ by depreciation

text.en: Divide the relevant income total by population. The average can increase without every household receiving more.

board.text: Per capita income is an average

text.en: If a shop produces the same number of loaves but charges more, its measured output value in current prices will rise.

board.text: Nominal GDP uses prices of the measured period

text.en: A simple way to understand real GDP is to value both periods’ output with the same set of prices. Then a price rise alone does not increase real output.

board.text: Real GDP separates output changes from price changes

text.en: Subtract the earlier real GDP from the later figure. Divide by the earlier figure and multiply by one hundred.

board.text: Use percentage change for growth

text.en: Ten loaves at one hundred rupees give one thousand. Twelve loaves at the same comparison price give one thousand two hundred, so real output has grown by twenty percent.

board.text: A worked comparison using bread

text.en: Growing crops, fishing and mining are examples of primary activities. They obtain products or materials directly from nature.

board.text: Primary activities obtain resources

text.en: Manufacturing converts inputs into products. Construction also belongs to the secondary sector in this school classification.

board.text: Secondary activities make goods or build structures

text.en: Transport, banking and teaching are examples. Goods production and services often support one another.

board.text: Tertiary activities provide services

text.en: Tamil Nadu’s G S D P describes production within the state. To compare years, check whether the prices are current or constant.

board.text: Gross State Domestic Product measures state output

text.en: Output growth is useful to measure. Development also concerns health, education, living standards and opportunities.

board.text: Growth and development answer different questions

text.en: GDP alone does not show who receives income, how much unpaid care people do, or how pollution changes. Other measures help answer those questions.

problem.en: A bakery sells a loaf for ₹100 after buying intermediate inputs costing ₹60. What does it add?

text.en: Subtract ₹60 of intermediate inputs from ₹100 of output.

why.en: The subtraction removes value added elsewhere in the supply chain.

text.en: The bakery adds ₹40 of value.

why.en: Adding value across producers avoids double-counting.

problem.en: Ten loaves at ₹100 become twelve loaves at ₹120. What is output growth at the old price?

text.en: Value the second year at the old price: 12 × ₹100 = ₹1,200.

why.en: Using common prices removes the effect of the price increase.

problem.en: Why can per capita income rise without gains for every household?

text.en: Per capita income is total income divided by population.

why.en: This computes an average, not a list of individual incomes.

text.en: An increase can be concentrated among some households.

why.en: Look at distribution as well as the average.

prompt.en: A friend says GDP counts only farm products. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: It counts all final goods and services.

points.en: GDP measures final output produced within an economy over a period.
GNP adjusts GDP by net primary income from the rest of the world.
Primary, secondary and tertiary activities all contribute to production.
